title: I Raised My Twin Daughters in Wheelchairs Alone After Their Mother Walked Out. Twelve Years Later, a Father's Day Secret Left Me Speechless
fb_text:
I raised my twin daughters, both in wheelchairs, completely on my own after their mother abandoned them... Twelve years later, the secret they revealed on Father's Day turned my world upside down!

I raised my twin girls, both of them in wheelchairs, without any help at all, after their mother left them when they were six years old. Twelve years later, on Father's Day, they looked at me with worry in their eyes and said: "Dad, promise us you won't get angry... We've been hiding something from you for a long time."

My name is Julien. For twelve years, my twin daughters, Élodie and Camille, have been the center of my life. I had to learn to be their father, their support and their only refuge when their mother decided to leave, while they were still little girls of six. They were born with a severe malformation of the spine and had always needed wheelchairs to get around. According to the doctors, their condition was incurable.

Just three months after their sixth birthday, their mother packed her bags. She told me bluntly that she didn't want to spend her whole life raising two disabled children. I will never forget that moment. I stared at her, stunned, unable to understand how she could turn her back on her own daughters without so much as a glance behind her.

Still, I didn't have the luxury of giving in to grief. My girls needed me, and I had to stay on my feet for them. Between rehabilitation sessions three times a week, medical appointments, school meetings and the endless repairs to their equipment, every day was a marathon. The expenses kept climbing, and exhaustion wore me down. But even on the days when I no longer had the strength to smile, I did my best to show them that everything would be all right.

I accepted every sacrifice that was needed. I worked, cooked the meals, kept the house running and learned how to use every device meant to make their daily lives easier. Little by little, I built a life in which my girls lacked neither love nor security. I wanted them to know one thing: even if their mother had abandoned them, their father never would.

The years went by, but I never remarried. I went on a few dates, but I never really tried to rebuild my love life. In the end, I stopped wondering what my life would be like without my girls. They were my priority, my happiness and my reason to keep going. I never saw the sacrifices I made as a burden.

Today, Élodie and Camille are eighteen.

This fall, they are getting ready to start at two different universities. Despite the hardships they have faced since birth, they have grown into ambitious, daring and independent young women. They learned to fight for their dreams, and they never allowed their disability to decide their future for them.

Then Father's Day arrived.

I expected a simple, happy day with them. Maybe they would make me breakfast, give me a touching card or hand me a gift they had made themselves, as they used to do when they were little. Those small surprises had always moved me deeply.

But this time, they had something else planned.

They asked me to come and sit at the kitchen table. Their manner struck me right away. They seemed nervous, almost afraid to speak to me.

Élodie exchanged a look with her sister. Camille took her hand and squeezed it gently, as if to give her the strength to go on.

After a few seconds of silence, Élodie turned to me.

"Dad, we need to talk to you. But please, don't be mad at us..."

My smile faded.

Camille continued in a hesitant voice:

"There's something we've been hiding from you for a while now. And, to be honest, we should have told you a long time ago."

My stomach knotted. My heart began to race as all kinds of worrying thoughts crowded my mind. What could they have done? What were they so afraid of? And why had they waited so long to tell me?

"What's going on? Why haven't you said anything until now?" I asked, more and more anxious.

They stayed silent. Then they looked at each other again, as if neither wanted to be the first to say the words that might change everything.

Suddenly, Élodie lowered her eyes to her bag, resting beside her wheelchair. Slowly, she slid her hand inside...

What she was about to reveal after twelve years of silence would leave me speechless.

article_html:
I raised my twin daughters, both in wheelchairs, completely on my own after their mother left. Twelve years later, on Father's Day, they told me they had been hiding something from me for a long time.

My name is Julien. For twelve years, my twin daughters, Élodie and Camille, have been the center of my life. When their mother decided to leave, they were only six years old, and I had to become their father, their support and their only refuge. They were born with a severe malformation of the spine and had always needed wheelchairs to get around. The doctors told us their condition was incurable.

The day she left

Just three months after their sixth birthday, their mother packed her bags. She told me bluntly that she didn't want to spend her whole life raising two disabled children. I stared at her, stunned, unable to understand how she could turn her back on her own daughters without looking back.

I didn't have the luxury of falling apart. Between rehabilitation three times a week, medical appointments, school meetings and constant repairs to their equipment, every day was a marathon. The bills kept growing, and exhaustion wore me down. Yet even on the days when I couldn't find the strength to smile, I made sure my girls believed everything would be all right.

I worked, cooked, ran the house and learned how to use every device that could make their lives easier. I wanted them to know one thing: their mother may have left, but their father never would. I never remarried. I went on a few dates, but my daughters were my priority, my happiness and my reason to keep going. I never saw my sacrifices as a burden.

Two young women

Today, Élodie and Camille are eighteen. This fall, they will start at two different universities. They have grown into ambitious, daring and independent young women who never let their disability decide their future for them.

On Father's Day, I expected a quiet, happy morning. Maybe breakfast, a card, a handmade gift like the ones they used to give me. Instead, they asked me to sit down at the kitchen table. They looked nervous, almost frightened.

Élodie glanced at her sister, and Camille squeezed her hand.

"Dad, we need to talk to you. But please, don't be mad at us..."

My smile disappeared.

"There's something we've been hiding from you for a while," Camille said softly. "We should have told you a long time ago."

My stomach knotted. "What's going on? Why haven't you said anything until now?"

They fell silent. Then Élodie lowered her eyes to the bag beside her wheelchair and slowly slid her hand inside.

The secret

She pulled out a thick folder and placed it in front of me. Camille took out an identical one.

"For the past three years, we've been working," Élodie said. "Online. Tutoring, translating, doing small design jobs. We didn't tell you because we knew you'd say we should focus on school and that you could handle everything."

I opened the first folder with trembling hands. Inside were acceptance letters from their universities, along with scholarship awards that covered most of their tuition. Beneath them was a savings statement. Every month, without a word to me, they had been setting money aside.

"We saw how much you gave up," Camille said, her voice breaking. "The overtime, the old car, the vacations you never took. We didn't want you to worry about paying for our future too."

"And the money?" I managed to ask.

Élodie smiled through her tears. "That's for you, Dad. We want you to finally take a real break. Rest. Travel. Do something just for yourself. You never left us. Now it's our turn to look after you."

I had been so afraid they were hiding something terrible. I wasn't angry at all. I was overwhelmed. Twelve years of exhaustion, worry and silent sacrifice seemed to melt away at that kitchen table. I pulled both of my daughters into my arms, and for a long time none of us could speak.

I did ask them one thing: to promise there would be no more secrets. They laughed and promised, and I laughed too, wiping my eyes.

That Father's Day, I understood something I had never dared to believe. I hadn't just raised two strong young women. I had raised two people who would never leave me alone either.

source.text:
J’ai élevé seul mes jumelles en fauteuil roulant après l’abandon de leur mère... Douze ans plus tard, leur secret révélé le jour des Pères m’a bouleversé !

J’ai élevé mes filles jumelles, toutes deux en fauteuil roulant, sans aucune aide, après que leur mère les a abandonnées à l’âge de six ans. Douze ans plus tard, le jour de la Fête des Pères, elles m’ont regardé avec inquiétude avant de me dire : « Papa, promets-nous de ne pas te mettre en colère… Cela fait longtemps que nous te cachons quelque chose. »

Je m’appelle Julien. Depuis douze ans, mes jumelles, Élodie et Camille, sont au centre de mon existence. J’ai dû apprendre à être à la fois leur père, leur soutien et leur unique refuge lorsque leur mère a décidé de partir, alors qu’elles n’étaient encore que des petites filles de six ans. Nées avec une grave malformation de la colonne vertébrale, elles avaient toujours eu besoin d’un fauteuil roulant pour se déplacer. Selon les médecins, leur état était incurable.

Trois mois seulement après leur sixième anniversaire, leur mère a fait ses valises. Elle m’a expliqué sans détour qu’elle ne voulait pas consacrer toute sa vie à élever deux enfants handicapés. Je n’oublierai jamais cet instant. Je la regardais, abasourdi, incapable de comprendre comment elle pouvait tourner le dos à ses propres filles sans même regarder en arrière.

Pourtant, je n’avais pas le luxe de m’abandonner au chagrin. Mes filles avaient besoin de moi, et je devais rester debout pour elles. Entre les séances de rééducation trois fois par semaine, les consultations médicales, les rendez-vous à l’école et les réparations incessantes de leurs équipements, chaque journée était un véritable marathon. Les dépenses ne cessaient d’augmenter, et la fatigue me rongeait. Mais, même les jours où je n’avais plus la force de sourire, je m’efforçais de leur montrer que tout irait bien.

J’ai accepté tous les sacrifices nécessaires. Je travaillais, je préparais les repas, je m’occupais de la maison et j’apprenais à utiliser chaque dispositif destiné à faciliter leur quotidien. Peu à peu, j’ai construit une vie dans laquelle mes filles ne manquaient ni d’amour ni de sécurité. Je voulais qu’elles sachent une chose : même si leur mère les avait abandonnées, leur père, lui, ne partirait jamais.

Les années ont passé, mais je ne me suis jamais remarié. J’ai eu quelques rendez-vous, sans jamais vraiment chercher à reconstruire ma vie sentimentale. Finalement, j’ai cessé de me demander ce que serait mon existence sans mes filles. Elles étaient ma priorité, mon bonheur et ma raison d’avancer. Je n’ai jamais considéré les sacrifices que j’avais faits comme un fardeau.

Aujourd’hui, Élodie et Camille ont dix-huit ans.

À la rentrée, elles s’apprêtent à rejoindre deux universités différentes. Malgré les difficultés rencontrées depuis leur naissance, elles sont devenues des jeunes femmes ambitieuses, audacieuses et autonomes. Elles ont appris à se battre pour leurs rêves et n’ont jamais accepté que leur handicap décide de leur avenir à leur place.

Puis la Fête des Pères est arrivée.

Je pensais passer une journée simple et heureuse avec elles. Peut-être m’auraient-elles préparé un petit-déjeuner, offert une carte touchante ou confectionné un cadeau de leurs propres mains, comme elles le faisaient autrefois. Ces petites surprises avaient toujours le pouvoir de m’émouvoir.

Mais cette fois, elles avaient prévu autre chose.

Elles m’ont demandé de venir m’asseoir à la table de la cuisine. Leur attitude m’a immédiatement intrigué. Elles semblaient nerveuses, presque effrayées à l’idée de me parler.

Élodie a échangé un regard avec sa sœur. Camille lui a alors pris la main et l’a serrée doucement, comme pour lui donner la force de continuer.

Après quelques secondes de silence, Élodie s’est tournée vers moi.

— Papa, il faut qu’on te parle. Mais, s’il te plaît, ne te fâche pas contre nous…

Mon sourire s’est effacé.

Camille a poursuivi d’une voix hésitante :

— Il y a quelque chose qu’on te cache depuis un bon moment. Et, pour être honnêtes, on aurait dû t’en parler depuis longtemps.

J’ai senti mon estomac se nouer. Mon cœur s’est emballé tandis que toutes sortes de pensées inquiétantes se bousculaient dans ma tête. Qu’avaient-elles pu faire ? De quoi avaient-elles si peur ? Et pourquoi avaient-elles attendu aussi longtemps pour m’en parler ?

— Qu’est-ce qui se passe ? Pourquoi ne m’avez-vous rien dit jusqu’à présent ? ai-je demandé, de plus en plus inquiet.

Elles sont restées silencieuses. Puis elles se sont regardées à nouveau, comme si aucune ne voulait être la première à prononcer les mots qui changeraient peut-être tout.

Soudain, Élodie a baissé les yeux vers son sac, posé près de son fauteuil roulant. Lentement, elle a glissé la main à l’intérieur…

Ce qu’elle s’apprêtait à me révéler après douze années de silence allait me laisser sans voix.
